raw_market_forces.raw_market_force_name: Easing Interest Rates and Regulatory Challenges
raw_market_forces.raw_description: After a period of high interest rates and regulatory scrutiny that inhibited M&A activity, 2025 is expected to see these pressures ease. Lower interest rates reduce the cost of capital, making borrowing and deal financing more attractive, while regulatory openness in the US, EU, UK, and India signals a more favorable environment for cross-border transactions. For the banking sector, this means increased deal flow, greater competition for assets, and a need to adapt to evolving compliance standards. The force is persistent, with medium- to long-term impact as monetary and regulatory cycles shift.

raw_findings.content: We expect that the two biggest inhibitors to deals in 2024—namely, interest rates and regulatory challenges—will ease in 2025.

New administrations in the EU and US are ushering more openness to M&A. Europe has signaled a desire for more pan-European industry champions... The UK Competition and Market Authority recently said it would favor behavioral remedies and revise its merger assessment process. India clarified merger guidelines and aimed to reduce approval timelines in 2024.

raw_examples.content: Europe has signaled a desire for more pan-European industry champions... The UK Competition and Market Authority recently said it would favor behavioral remedies and revise its merger assessment process.

relevant_facts.content: Interest rates and regulatory scrutiny were the two fiercest M&A headwinds in 2024.

relevant_statistics.content: Global M&A as a percentage of nominal GDP has lingered at nearly 30-year lows.

relevant_quotes.content: We expect that the two biggest inhibitors to deals in 2024—namely, interest rates and regulatory challenges—will ease in 2025.

possible_structural_shifts: Shift toward more cross-border banking M&A
implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks may see increased opportunities for inorganic growth.
Compliance teams must adapt to evolving regulatory standards.
Lower financing costs could spur consolidation and expansion.

sources.title: Looking Ahead to 2025: Preparing for What Comes Next

raw_market_forces.raw_description: Long-term technological shifts, especially the rise of generative AI, automation, renewable energy, and quantum computing, are driving strategic transformation across industries, including banking. Banks must invest in or acquire new technologies to remain competitive, manage risk, and prevent fraud. The rapid pace of innovation and the need for early-stage investments or partnerships in AI assets are reshaping M&A strategies and operational models in the sector.

raw_findings.content: Technology disruption. It’s the long-term shift that will result in the most strategic transformation and M&A in the years ahead. Generative AI/AI, automation, renewable energy, and quantum computing are just a few of the technologies that companies will need to build or buy to maintain competitive offerings and cost positions.

raw_examples.content: Visa acquired Featurespace, an AI-native transaction monitoring company that will enable cutting-edge fraud and financial crime prevention.

relevant_facts.content: Over the past six years, non-tech companies were the buyers in one in every three strategic tech deals worth more than $100 million.

relevant_statistics.content: 70% of private equity companies have killed a deal when a likely negative impact of generative AI on the target’s business model became clear.

relevant_quotes.content: Generative AI is already transforming M&A work. The benefits are accruing to early adopters and frequent acquirers, and the value gained from AI tools grows with user sophistication.

implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks must accelerate technology adoption to remain competitive.
AI-driven fraud prevention and risk management will become standard.
Early-stage investments and partnerships in AI will shape future banking models.

raw_market_forces.raw_description: The global economic landscape is shifting from a bipolar (transatlantic/China) to a multipolar (US/EU/China) dynamic. National economic interests are being reasserted through reviews of foreign direct investment, M&A activity, and tariff policies. Geopolitical uncertainty, trade tensions, and national industrial policies are prompting banks to reevaluate their global footprints, supply chains, and market access strategies. This force is persistent and will shape cross-border banking, risk management, and growth opportunities for years to come.

raw_findings.content: National economic interests are being reasserted through reviews of foreign direct investment and M&A activity on national interest grounds—and tariff policies, too.

raw_examples.content: To prepare for the second Trump administration’s proposed move to stiffen tariffs, executives are reevaluating global footprints to ensure access to attractive end markets and security of supply, which could prompt both acquisition and divestiture activity.

relevant_facts.content: The world is moving from a bipolar (transatlantic/China) to multipolar (US/EU/China) dynamic.

relevant_quotes.content: National economic interests are being reasserted through reviews of foreign direct investment and M&A activity on national interest grounds—and tariff policies, too.

possible_signals: Increased regulatory reviews of cross-border deals
Banks exiting or entering new markets
implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks must adapt to shifting trade and investment policies.
Cross-border M&A will require more sophisticated risk assessment.
Geopolitical uncertainty will drive strategic realignment of banking operations.

raw_market_forces.raw_market_force_name: Shifting Profit Pools and Sector Realignment
raw_market_forces.raw_description: Profit pools are shifting across sectors due to technology, consolidation, and changing consumer behavior. In banking, this means a need to adapt strategies to capture emerging value, divest non-core assets, and pursue new growth areas. The force is persistent, as sector boundaries blur and new competitors emerge, requiring banks to continually reassess their portfolios and business models.

raw_findings.content: M&A enables companies to adapt their strategies toward shifting profit pools of all types.

raw_examples.content: In consolidated sectors such as consumer products, the largest players reshape and focus on their parenting advantage by shedding assets.

relevant_facts.content: Media companies are reaching across sectors, acquiring to build up evergreen content libraries to compete against technology mega-platforms.

relevant_quotes.content: M&A enables companies to adapt their strategies toward shifting profit pools of all types.

possible_signals: Entry into new financial services segments
implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks must continually reassess and realign their portfolios.
New profit pools may emerge in fintech, payments, and digital assets.
Divestitures and acquisitions will be key to maintaining competitiveness.

raw_market_forces.raw_market_force_name: Alternative Deal Structures and Risk Mitigation
raw_market_forces.raw_description: High costs, uncertainty, and rapid technological change are driving companies—including banks—to pursue alternative deal structures such as minority stakes, joint ventures, partnerships, and licensing arrangements. These structures allow for risk mitigation and flexibility, especially in emerging technologies or volatile markets. The trend is persistent and gaining momentum as leadership teams seek to hedge bets and maintain optionality in uncertain environments.

raw_findings.content: When an outright acquisition isn’t justified, more companies are hedging their bets by taking minority stakes or engaging in joint ventures, partnerships, or licensing arrangements.

raw_examples.content: The moves are most attractive during times of high cost and high uncertainty, such as an emerging technology without a defined standard—that applies to everything from generative AI to electric vehicle batteries.

relevant_facts.content: The combination of economic weakness, changes in geopolitics and national industrial policies, tech disruptions, and valuation gaps between buyers and sellers all contribute to the uncertainty and indecision that may make alternative deal types more attractive.

relevant_quotes.content: When an outright acquisition isn’t justified, more companies are hedging their bets by taking minority stakes or engaging in joint ventures, partnerships, or licensing arrangements.

implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks will use alternative deal structures to access innovation and manage risk.
Joint ventures and partnerships will become more common in fintech and digital banking.
Minority stakes allow banks to participate in emerging sectors without full exposure.

raw_market_forces.raw_description: Banks globally are under increasing pressure to modernize their technology infrastructure and digitize operations. This is driven by the need to remain competitive, manage costs, and meet evolving customer expectations. The high cost of technology modernization, coupled with the rapid pace of digital innovation, is pushing banks toward scale transactions and M&A to share technology investments and deliver cost synergies. This force is persistent and is reshaping the competitive landscape in banking, payments, and wealth management.

raw_findings.content: Banks are under pressure to keep costs under control as they grapple with the high cost of technology modernization as well as general inflation. In 2024, banks with an eye on profitability and a desire to defray technology investment costs turned to scale transactions to deliver meaningful cost synergies.

raw_examples.content: The announced more than $35 billion Capital One–Discover deal in the US, a move that spanned both the banking and payments sectors and that promised at least $2.7 billion in synergies.

relevant_facts.content: Banking M&A rebounded, with 215 deals greater than $30 million in value announced by December 2024 compared with 151 deals announced during the same period in 2023.

relevant_statistics.content: Bank executives are openly signaling interest in M&A: The number of banks open to acquiring or actively pursuing acquisitions jumped almost threefold among the top 50 US banks in 2024 vs. 2023 and fourfold among Europe’s top 25 banks.

relevant_quotes.content: Banks will acquire for scale leadership and to share technology investments.

possible_signals: Increased M&A activity focused on technology
possible_structural_shifts: Shift toward fewer, larger banks with advanced digital capabilities
implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks unable to keep pace with technology modernization may become acquisition targets.
Scale and technology sharing will become critical for profitability and competitiveness.

raw_market_forces.raw_description: Changes in regulatory policy, especially in the US and Europe, are a significant external force shaping banking sector M&A and strategic decisions. The expectation of a more relaxed US regulatory environment under a new federal administration is anticipated to accelerate M&A activity, while European banks face pressure to consolidate and improve efficiency. Regulatory shifts also impact insurance and brokerage consolidation, with potential for further reshuffling if regulations become more favorable.

raw_findings.content: In the US, a more ambitious M&A agenda may be easier to pursue under the new federal administration, which is expected to be more open to banking sector M&A and to relax US banking regulations.

raw_examples.content: If a more favorable regulatory environment emerges, especially in the US, we will see a continued reshuffling of the brokerage leaderboards across markets.

relevant_facts.content: The potential for a more relaxed US regulatory environment will put more urgency on European banks to strengthen their competitive positions and improve efficiency and profitability via consolidation.

relevant_quotes.content: The message for banks: There’s an urgency to act. Be proactive in identifying potential acquirees that will deliver leadership economics, and be prepared to articulate ambitious cost synergy targets to be competitive in a consolidating market.

possible_structural_shifts: Greater consolidation in US and European banking sectors
implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks may accelerate M&A to preempt regulatory changes.
Regulatory shifts could alter the competitive landscape and enable new entrants or larger players.

raw_market_forces.raw_description: The rapid digitization of payments is a major force driving M&A and innovation in the banking sector. Payment incumbents are acquiring to accelerate innovation, expand capabilities, and build out infrastructure. Fraud prevention and identity verification have become critical investment areas due to evolving fraud risks, including AI-driven scams and deepfakes. This force is persistent and is expected to drive further M&A and technology investment in the sector.

raw_findings.content: Now, payment incumbents across all regions are using M&A to meet a variety of ends as they ride the wave of payments digitization. Fraud prevention and identity verification are particularly hot areas for activity, as highlighted by acquisitions by Mastercard, Visa, and Socure.

raw_examples.content: The Capital One–Discover deal has the potential to realign competitive dynamics in the US, and the Stripe purchase of Bridge puts stablecoin back on the map.

relevant_facts.content: Evolving fraud risks—particularly as authorized push payment scams intensify and generative AI fuels deepfakes—ensure that fraud prevention and identity verification will be a long-term investment vector.

relevant_statistics.content: 11-month total deal value across financial services was 72% higher than during the same 11-month period in 2023.

relevant_quotes.content: In payments, fraud prevention and identity verification will be among the hot areas for acquisitions.

possible_signals: Banks investing in identity verification technologies
implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks and payment firms must invest in fraud prevention to maintain trust.
Failure to innovate in payments could result in loss of market share.

raw_market_forces.raw_market_force_name: Portfolio Reshaping and Divestitures in Insurance and Banking
raw_market_forces.raw_description: Ongoing portfolio reshaping, including divestitures and exits from noncore or underperforming lines, is a significant force in banking and insurance. This is driven by the need to recover from underwriting challenges, balance sheet impairments, and ratings downgrades. Geographic and product portfolio optimization is expected to continue, with multinationals reassessing capital allocation and growth potential.

raw_findings.content: Portfolio reshaping, a characteristic of 2024, will continue into 2025, with carriers working their way out of troubled underwriting positions, balance sheet impairments, and ratings downgrades.

raw_examples.content: Allstate and its exit of the employer voluntary benefits business. Allianz’s divestiture of its US MidCorp and Entertainment businesses.

relevant_facts.content: Deal value rose slightly, at $77 billion by December 2024 compared with $50 billion in December 2023, even as deal volume declined to only 72 deals during the period compared with 95 for 2023.

relevant_quotes.content: Insurers will use M&A to refocus on core lines of business.

implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks and insurers will continue to shed noncore assets.

raw_market_forces.raw_market_force_name: Rise of Private Markets and Alternative Asset Management
raw_market_forces.raw_description: The rapid growth of private markets and alternative asset managers is reshaping the wealth and asset management landscape. Traditional asset managers and universal banks are aggressively acquiring or partnering to move into private markets, while alternative asset managers seek scale. This trend is driving a revival in M&A and joint ventures, with implications for competition and product offerings in banking and wealth management.

raw_findings.content: The success of asset managers with a private market focus is quickly redefining the playing field in wealth and asset management—and sparking a revival in M&A and joint ventures.

raw_examples.content: BlackRock announced that it will buy HPS Investment Partners for $12 billion to expand its offerings in the private credit market.

relevant_facts.content: Alternative asset manager Apollo formed a $25 billion exclusive partnership with Citigroup to combine Citi's extensive client network and banking capabilities with Apollo's deep capital resources and expertise in private credit investments.

relevant_statistics.content: Alternative asset managers that invest in the capital of privately owned companies have watched their market cap grow by more than 4 times over the past five years compared with a 1.6 times market cap growth for traditional asset managers.

relevant_quotes.content: In wealth and asset management, deals will continue to grow private market offerings.

possible_signals: Growth in private market product launches
possible_structural_shifts: Blurring of lines between traditional and alternative asset management
implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks and asset managers must adapt to compete in private markets.
Failure to enter private markets may result in loss of competitiveness.

raw_market_forces.raw_market_force_name: Extreme Market Volatility and Economic Uncertainty
raw_market_forces.raw_description: The global asset management and banking sectors are increasingly exposed to extreme market volatility and heightened economic uncertainty. This is driven by rapid shifts in investor sentiment, disruptive geopolitical events (such as US tariffs), and broader macroeconomic instability. These external conditions have a direct impact on revenue growth, asset flows, and risk management strategies, requiring firms to adapt quickly to unpredictable environments. The persistence and momentum of these forces are evidenced by the significant role market performance played in revenue growth (70% in 2024), highlighting the vulnerability of the sector to external shocks.

raw_findings.content: Market performance drove 70% of revenue growth in 2024, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability to external conditions—especially in a period marked by extreme market volatility, rapid shifts in sentiment, and heightened economic uncertainty arising in part from the disruptive effects of the US tariffs.

raw_examples.content: Major indexes such as the S&P 500 (up 23% for the year) and NASDAQ (up 29%) rose significantly, but these gains are attributed to volatile market conditions.

relevant_facts.content: Global asset management industry reached a record $128 trillion in assets under management (AuM) in 2024, up 12% from the previous year.

relevant_statistics.content: 70% of revenue growth in 2024 was driven by market performance.

relevant_data.content: Global revenues for the industry rose by $58 billion, and more than 70% ($42 billion) of that gain came from market performance.

relevant_quotes.content: The industry’s vulnerability to external conditions—especially in a period marked by extreme market volatility, rapid shifts in sentiment, and heightened economic uncertainty arising in part from the disruptive effects of the US tariffs.

possible_structural_shifts: Shift to more resilient business models
implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks and asset managers must enhance risk management frameworks.
Increased demand for scenario planning and stress testing.
Potential for regulatory changes to address systemic risks.

raw_market_forces.raw_market_force_name: Shifts in Investor Preferences Toward Low-Cost and Passive Products
raw_market_forces.raw_description: There is a persistent and accelerating shift in investor preferences from actively managed funds to low-cost, efficient products such as exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and passive investment vehicles. This trend is driven by both retail and institutional investors seeking lower fees and greater transparency. The momentum is evidenced by significant net inflows into passive funds and outflows from active funds, as well as the growing share of passive AuM globally. This shift is reshaping product development, distribution strategies, and competitive dynamics in the banking and asset management sectors.

raw_findings.content: Last year, investors continued a long-term trend of shifting from actively managed funds to passively managed products. Active AuM declined from 65% in 2023 to 61% in 2024 for mutual funds and ETFs.

raw_examples.content: Net new flows reflected this trend, with $0.1 trillion in outflows from active funds, excluding money market funds, versus $1.6 trillion in inflows to passive funds.

relevant_facts.content: Passive AuM grew from 17% to 20% of assets while active AuM shrank from 44% to 38% of assets over the past five years.

relevant_statistics.content: $1.6 trillion in inflows to passive funds versus $0.1 trillion in outflows from active funds in 2024.

relevant_data.content: Fees on 2024 net inflows were, on average, about 40 basis points less than fees on 2023 existing AuM across mutual funds and ETFs.

relevant_quotes.content: Investors are demanding low-cost, efficient products such as exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

possible_structural_shifts: Greater focus on scale and efficiency
implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks and asset managers must innovate to offer competitive, low-cost products.
Potential for further fee compression and margin pressure.
Need for differentiated value propositions beyond performance.

raw_market_forces.raw_description: Amidst ongoing pricing pressures and a shifting market landscape, banks and asset managers are under increasing pressure to radically reduce costs. These changes are persistent and are fundamentally altering operational models, workforce composition, and the competitive dynamics of the sector.

raw_findings.content: Cost structures need to be radically leaner. Many firms are increasingly adopting one of three strategic models to shape their cost structures—focusing their spending on investment management and trade execution; sales, marketing, and operations; or IT.

raw_examples.content: This approach entails reexamining all costs and may lead to such changes as outsourcing noncore functions, automating processes with generative AI (GenAI), and avoiding dual-run costs, especially in headcount.

raw_market_forces.raw_description: Deglobalization refers to the accelerating retreat from globalization, driven by trade tensions, geopolitical rivalries, and reassessment of supply chain vulnerabilities. This trend is characterized by increased economic nationalism, trade regionalization, and a surge in trade restrictions (from 1,000 in 2019 to over 3,000 in 2023). Deglobalization challenges economic growth, increases inflationary pressures, reduces efficiency gains, and fragments financial markets, constraining cross-border capital flows and increasing macro-financial volatility. The effects are uneven, with emerging and developing economies disproportionately impacted due to their reliance on foreign direct investment and exposure to commodity supply risks. For the banking sector, deglobalization means greater volatility, increased compliance complexity, and the need to adapt to shifting capital flows and regional market structures.

Decarbonization is inflationary, as adaptation spending does not immediately increase productivity or the tax base. raw_market_forces.raw_description: The increasing fragmentation of the global geopolitical landscape, with rising tensions between major powers and the emergence of competing blocs, is reshaping the environment in which banks operate. This multipolarity leads to divergent regulatory regimes, cross-border transaction complexities, and heightened sanctions risks. For the banking sector, this means greater uncertainty in international operations, increased compliance costs, and potential disruptions to global capital flows.

raw_findings.content: The report highlights a world of growing divisions, with geopolitical tensions and the formation of competing blocs impacting global cooperation and economic stability.

raw_examples.content: Banks facing increased due diligence requirements for cross-border transactions due to sanctions and regulatory divergence.

relevant_facts.content: Geopolitical fragmentation is cited as a top risk for 2025, with direct implications for global financial flows.

relevant_quotes.content: "A world of growing divisions is likely to see more fragmented regulatory environments and increased risk for cross-border financial institutions."

implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks must adapt to a more complex regulatory landscape and manage increased geopolitical risk in cross-border operations.

raw_market_forces.raw_description: Persistent economic instability, characterized by high inflation, rising interest rates, and mounting public and private debt, is a significant market force for the banking sector. These conditions increase credit risk, reduce lending activity, and threaten the solvency of both borrowers and financial institutions. Banks must navigate volatile markets and prepare for potential defaults and liquidity crunches.

raw_findings.content: The report identifies economic instability and debt vulnerabilities as key risks, with implications for financial sector stability.

raw_examples.content: Banks tightening lending standards in response to rising defaults and economic uncertainty.

relevant_facts.content: High levels of public and private debt are cited as vulnerabilities that could trigger financial instability.

relevant_quotes.content: "Economic instability and debt vulnerabilities remain persistent risks for the global financial system."

implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks will need to strengthen risk management and prepare for potential shocks to credit markets.

raw_market_forces.raw_description: Rapid technological advancements, including the proliferation of artificial intelligence, digital currencies, and fintech innovation, are transforming the banking sector. At the same time, the sector faces escalating cybersecurity threats and risks of systemic disruption. Banks must invest in digital infrastructure, enhance cyber resilience, and adapt to new competitive dynamics from non-traditional financial players.

raw_findings.content: The report notes that technological disruption and cyber risks are accelerating, with direct impacts on financial services.

raw_examples.content: Banks experiencing increased cyberattacks and investing in AI-driven fraud detection.

relevant_facts.content: Cybersecurity threats are among the top risks for the financial sector in 2025.

relevant_quotes.content: "Technological disruption and cyber risks are accelerating, requiring banks to adapt rapidly."

implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks must prioritize cybersecurity and digital innovation to remain competitive and resilient.

raw_market_forces.raw_description: Climate change and related environmental risks are increasingly shaping the banking sector's risk landscape. Physical risks from extreme weather events, as well as transition risks from regulatory and market shifts towards sustainability, are impacting asset valuations, lending practices, and regulatory compliance. Banks are under pressure to align portfolios with climate goals and manage exposure to carbon-intensive sectors.

raw_findings.content: The report identifies climate change as a persistent and escalating risk, with direct implications for financial stability.

raw_examples.content: Banks integrating climate risk assessments into lending and investment decisions.

relevant_facts.content: Climate-related risks are expected to persist and intensify, affecting asset values and regulatory requirements.

relevant_quotes.content: "Climate change and environmental risks are increasingly shaping the financial sector's risk landscape."

implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks must integrate climate risk into strategy and comply with evolving environmental regulations.

raw_market_forces.raw_description: Diverging regulatory standards across jurisdictions, driven by geopolitical fragmentation and differing national priorities, are increasing compliance complexity for global banks. This market force requires banks to invest more in compliance infrastructure, adapt to local requirements, and manage the risk of regulatory arbitrage and enforcement actions.

raw_findings.content: The report notes that regulatory divergence is a growing challenge for multinational banks.

raw_examples.content: Banks establishing separate compliance teams for different regions to meet local regulatory requirements.

relevant_facts.content: Regulatory divergence increases operational costs and complexity for global financial institutions.

relevant_quotes.content: "Diverging regulatory standards are a growing challenge for multinational banks."

implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks must enhance compliance capabilities and adapt to a patchwork of global regulations.

raw_market_forces.raw_market_force_name: Societal Polarization and Erosion of Trust
raw_market_forces.raw_description: Rising societal polarization, misinformation, and declining trust in institutions are shaping the operating environment for banks. This market force can lead to increased regulatory scrutiny, reputational risks, and challenges in customer engagement. Banks must navigate shifting public expectations and demonstrate social responsibility to maintain legitimacy.

raw_findings.content: The report highlights societal polarization and declining trust as persistent risks with implications for the financial sector.

raw_examples.content: Banks facing public backlash over perceived ethical lapses or social issues.

relevant_facts.content: Societal polarization can increase regulatory and reputational risks for banks.

relevant_quotes.content: "Societal polarization and declining trust in institutions are persistent risks for the financial sector."

implications_on_future_of_sector: Banks must build trust and demonstrate social responsibility to maintain their social license to operate.
